content: Less than or equal to 2% of men aged 20 years or older and 2% of women aged 50 years or older were found to have iron-deficiency anemia, as shown in Table 4. Data from the Continuing Survey of Food Intakes by Individuals (CFSII) indicate that the majority of men and women aged 50 years or older meet the recommended dietary allowance for iron through their diet, as presented in Table 5. In a study of adults with iron-deficiency anemia, 62% exhibited clinical evidence of gastrointestinal bleeding caused by lesions, such as ulcers and tumors. According to the first National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES I), conducted between 1971 and 1975, approximately two-thirds of anemia cases in men and postmenopausal women were attributed to chronic diseases or inflammatory conditions. These findings suggest that, in these populations, the primary causes of anemia are chronic diseases and inflammatory conditions, rather than low dietary iron intake. Iron status can be evaluated using various laboratory tests. Each test assesses a different aspect of iron metabolism, and the results of one test may not always align with those of another. Hematological tests, which are based on red blood cell characteristics (e.g., hemoglobin concentration, hematocrit, mean cell volume, and red blood cell distribution width), are generally more accessible and less expensive than biochemical tests. However, biochemical tests, such as erythrocyte protoporphyrin concentration, serum ferritin concentration, and transferrin saturation, are capable of detecting earlier changes in iron status. Despite the availability of these tests, no single test is universally accepted for diagnosing iron deficiency. Detecting iron deficiency in clinical or field settings is more complex than commonly perceived, due to a lack of standardization among tests and limited laboratory proficiency testing, which complicates the comparison of results across laboratories. Laboratory proficiency testing is currently available for measuring hemoglobin concentration, hematocrit, red blood cell count, serum ferritin concentration, and serum iron concentration. In 1997, provisional proficiency testing for total iron-binding capacity was introduced in the College of American Pathologists survey and added to the American Association of Bioanalysts survey in 1998. As of April 1998, three states (New York, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin) had proficiency testing programs for erythrocyte protoporphyrin concentration. Regardless of whether test standardization and proficiency testing become routine, healthcare providers must develop a better understanding of the strengths and limitations of each test to improve screening and diagnosis of iron-deficiency anemia. This is particularly important because the results of these tests can be influenced by factors other than iron status. The most commonly used tests for screening iron deficiency are hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit, due to their low cost and ease of use. Hematocrit reflects the proportion of whole blood occupied by red blood cells and decreases only after hemoglobin concentration falls. However, because changes in hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit occur only in the later stages of iron deficiency, these tests are considered late indicators of iron deficiency. Nevertheless, they are essential for diagnosing iron-deficiency anemia. Iron deficiency is a common cause of childhood anemia, leading to the interchangeable use of the terms anemia, iron deficiency, and iron-deficiency anemia. However, only cases of anemia with additional evidence of iron deficiency can be classified as iron-deficiency anemia. The association between anemia and iron deficiency is most accurate in populations with a high prevalence of iron deficiency. In the United States, the prevalence and severity of anemia have declined in recent years, resulting in an increased proportion of anemia cases caused by factors other than iron deficiency. Consequently, the effectiveness of anemia screening for detecting iron deficiency has decreased in the United States. Iron deficiency can be defined by absent bone marrow iron stores (as observed on bone marrow iron smears), an increase in hemoglobin concentration of more than 1.0 g/dL after iron treatment, or abnormal values on certain biochemical tests. Recent recognition of the potentially serious negative effects of iron deficiency has emphasized the importance of identifying individuals with iron deficiency, even in the absence of anemia. The case definition of anemia recommended in this report is a hemoglobin concentration or hematocrit below the 5th percentile of the distribution in a healthy reference population, adjusted for age, sex, and pregnancy stage (for pregnant women). This definition has been shown to correctly identify 37% of women of childbearing age and 25% of children aged 1–5 years who were iron deficient (sensitivity) and to correctly classify 93% of women of childbearing age and 92% of children aged 1–5 years as not having iron deficiency (specificity). Lowering the hemoglobin concentration or hematocrit cutoff would reduce the number of false positives (anemia cases due to causes other than iron deficiency) but would also overlook more true positives (individuals with iron deficiency). The distributions of hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit, and thus the cutoff values for anemia, vary by age, sex, pregnancy status, altitude, smoking status, and race. Among pregnant women, hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit decline during the first and second trimesters due to expanding blood volume. In women who do not take iron supplements, these values remain low in the third trimester. In contrast, pregnant women with adequate iron intake experience a gradual rise in hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit during the third trimester, approaching pre-pregnancy levels. Due to a lack of adequate U.S. data, anemia cutoff values are based on clinical studies of European women who took iron supplements during pregnancy. For pregnant women, a hemoglobin concentration greater than 15.0 g/dL or a hematocrit greater than 45.0%, particularly in the second trimester, likely indicates poor blood volume expansion. High hemoglobin concentration or hematocrit has been associated with hypertension and adverse pregnancy outcomes, such as fetal growth retardation, fetal death, preterm delivery, and low birth weight. For example, women with a hematocrit of 43% or higher at 26–30 weeks of gestation had more than twice the risk of preterm delivery and four times the risk of delivering a child with fetal growth retardation compared to women with a hematocrit of 33%–36%. Therefore, high hemoglobin concentration or hematocrit in the second or third trimester of pregnancy should not be considered an indicator of desirable iron status.
